full_text: News Дата публікації: November 9, 2026 In the First Nine Months of 2026, Municipalities’ Own Revenues Grew by 11.1%, While Russian Attacks Increased by 44.4% Year-on-Year — KSE Institute Municipal Review Published: November 9, 2026 Read the full material Analytical product KSE Institute Read the full material In the first nine months of 2026, municipalities’ own general fund revenues, excluding transfers, reached $7.4 billion, up 11.1% in US dollar terms and 17.7% in hryvnia compared with the same period last year. However, significant regional disparities persisted. Revenues declined by 24.1% in Donetsk Oblast and 4.2% in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, while most other regions recorded growth. Despite rising revenues, municipalities reduced capital spending and faced an increasing number of Russian attacks. These findings are presented in the Municipal Review for the first nine months of 2026, prepared by the Center for Public Finance and Governance Analysis at KSE Institute together with KSE University. Personal income tax (PIT) remained the largest source of municipalities’ own revenues. It generated $4 billion, up 14.3% year-on-year, and accounted for 54.2% of total revenues. Unified tax receipts reached $1.1 billion (+5.3%), although the number of registered individual entrepreneurs exceeded 2.2 million. Land fee revenues amounted to $740.5 million (+6.8%), excise tax revenues to $608.6 million (+11.2%), and real estate tax revenues to $193.5 million (+7.6%). Revenue growth from several sources slowed compared with the first half of the year. The situation remained particularly difficult for municipalities losing residents, businesses and land due to the war. Transfers from the state budget increased by 34.1%, largely reflecting additional funding for responsibilities already assigned to municipalities. The education subvention rose by 31% following increases in teachers’ salaries, while the basic equalisation grant grew by 14.4%. At the same time, the additional grant for municipalities most affected by the war declined by 22.5% year-on-year. In the draft 2027 State Budget, the Government also proposed reducing the municipal share of PIT from 64% to 60%. Following the first reading on 28 October, Parliament instructed the Government to consider retaining the 64% share and allowing municipalities to keep the reverse equalisation grant. Total municipal expenditures reached $10 billion, up 13% year-on-year. Education accounted for 48% of all spending, while housing and communal services represented 10.5%. Current expenditures increased by 16% to $8.9 billion, accounting for 88.4% of total spending. Capital expenditures fell by 5.9% to $1.1 billion, while transfers to development budgets declined by 57.4%. In September, municipalities also faced Treasury payment delays affecting utility services, repairs, civil protection measures and recovery projects. full_text: News Дата публікації: November 6, 2026 Russian LNG Tracker – Q3 2026: Sanctioned tankers carried more than a quarter of Russia’s LNG exports Published: November 6, 2026 Download the full report Analytical product KSE Institute Download the full report In Q3 2026, 22 sanctioned LNG tankers transported 2.1 million tonnes of Russian LNG. That is more than 26% of Russia’s total seaborne LNG exports for the quarter and 37% of the active LNG tanker fleet loading in Russia. The findings come from the new edition of KSE Institute’s Russian LNG Tracker. Global seaborne LNG exports reached 33.8 million tonnes in September. The United States remained the largest exporter with a 31% share, while Russia ranked third with 10%. Russia’s seaborne LNG exports rose 51% month-on-month to 3.4 million tonnes, driven by higher shipments from the Yamal LNG and Sakhalin 2 terminals. Both likely returned to normal operations after maintenance. Yamal LNG continues to dominate Russian LNG exports, accounting for 46% of volumes in September. Between January and September 2026, Russia exported 12.0 million tonnes of LNG to the EU, up 7.8% year-on-year. The EU received 47% of Russia’s total LNG exports, with France accounting for 40% of EU-bound volumes. In September, China and France together imported 60% of Russian LNG. In September, tankers linked exclusively to companies outside EU/G7 jurisdictions carried 59% of Russian LNG. These vessels mainly supplied China (55%) and South Korea (13%). Ship managers based in Japan and Russia handled 47% of Russian LNG shipments in September. The same share was carried by tankers whose registered owners are based in these two countries. ISM managers from Singapore and Russia oversaw vessels that carried 67% of total volumes. The share of Russia-flagged tankers in Russia’s total seaborne LNG exports rose from 3% in March to 26% in September 2026. In September, 44 unique tankers transported Russian LNG, up from 30 in August. During July-September, the top ten ship management companies accounted for an average of 88% of Russia’s LNG exports. The top three companies stayed the same throughout the period. They were Seapeak Maritime Singapore (Singapore), Mitsui Osk Lines Ltd (Japan) and Dynagas Ltd (Greece), and together they carried an average of 53% of Russia’s monthly LNG exports. full_text: News Дата публікації: November 4, 2026 Net Support to Ukrainian Farmers Averaged Just 0.1% of Gross Farm Receipts in 2023-2025, Compared with 14.3% Across OECD Countries — KSE Institute Published: November 4, 2026 Read the full report Research KSE Institute Read the full report Support to agricultural producers in Ukraine averaged 0.1% of gross farm receipts in 2023–2025, compared with 14.3% across countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). The figures are presented in the new report, “Agricultural Policy Monitoring and Evaluation 2026: Enhancing Resilience in a World of Interconnected Risks”, which examines agricultural policies in 56 countries. Analysts from the Center for Food and Land Use Research (KSE Agrocenter) contributed data and analytical material to the Ukraine chapter. Agricultural producer support reflects government payments, tax concessions, and the effects of agricultural policies on producer prices. In Ukraine, this indicator has remained close to zero in recent years. It stood at −1.16% of gross farm receipts in 2023, increased to 0.62% in 2024, and reached 0.64% in 2025. Export restrictions affect these figures by reducing the prices farmers can receive for their products relative to international markets. Over the past decade, domestic prices for oats, rye, sunflower, and milk in Ukraine have generally remained below international reference prices. Export restrictions have been an important factor for oats, rye, and sunflower, while market conditions have played a greater role in milk prices. Import tariffs on sugar and pig meat, by contrast, have helped maintain domestic prices above international levels. In 2023–2025, market price support and subsidies for the use of variable inputs without restrictions accounted for 40% of transfers to farmers. The OECD identifies these measures as among those with the greatest potential to distort agricultural production and trade. The gap between Ukraine and other countries is particularly pronounced in public spending on agricultural research, infrastructure, and services. In 2023–2025, support for these purposes amounted to 0.8% of agricultural production value in Ukraine, compared with an average of 2.4% across the countries covered by the report. Most of Ukraine’s spending was directed towards inspection and control. Expenditure on agricultural knowledge and innovation has fallen by more than half relative to the sector’s size, while infrastructure spending has declined to a near-zero share of production value. Total support to agriculture amounted to 0.2% of GDP in 2023–2025, down from 0.4% two decades earlier. In 2025–2026, Ukraine continued supporting agricultural producers operating under wartime conditions. The working-capital component of the Affordable Loans “5-7-9%” programme was extended until March 2027. Two consecutive monthly budget surpluses helped narrow the cumulative deficit, although fiscal pressures remain significant. The average Russian oil export price climbed from $68.4 to $93.3 per barrel, while the discount to global benchmarks widened slightly to $23.6 per barrel. Total crude oil and petroleum product exports remained at 6.5 million barrels per day, their lowest level since the start of the full-scale invasion. Following the reopening of ports, crude shipments edged up from 5.2 to 5.3 million barrels per day, while petroleum product exports shrunk to a new record low of 1.2 million barrels per day due to continued refinery strikes and export bans. The cumulative deficit narrowed from 5.8 trillion to 5.2 trillion rubles but already accounts for 71% of the newly approved full-year target of 7.3 trillion rubles. Over January-September, oil and gas budget revenues fell 17% year-on-year, partly because higher oil prices increased damper reimbursements. These payments reached 400 billion rubles in September. To cover its financing needs, the Ministry of Finance returned to domestic borrowing after a two-month pause, raising 1.3 trillion rubles in September – the highest monthly amount since November 2025. Nezir Sinani, Executive Director of the B4Ukraine Coalition, said: “Russia’s systematic expropriation of EU companies and contributions to the Russian military underscore a fundamental miscalculation by both businesses and policymakers: the belief that business as usual was possible and that Russia would not weaponise their continued presence in the country. The Kremlin can transfer control of their businesses to Russian entities, leaving the owners with little say over what happens next. METRO is a clear example. title: Genuine Social Inclusion Instead of Cash Benefits: What Ukraine Needs to Do on Its Path to the EU
summary: The Commission again identifies social benefits reform as a key priority. It considers the level of support insufficient, especially for people with disabilities and those in vulnerable situations.

full_text: Reforms November 9, 2026 Genuine Social Inclusion Instead of Cash Benefits: What Ukraine Needs to Do on Its Path to the EU Mariia Balytska Reforms Photo: unsplash.com / Guillaume Périgois November 9, 2026 Facebook X Telegram 6 The main idea behind the EU’s approach to social policy is simple: helping people is not just about providing money. Above all, it is about enabling them to become self-reliant. This is the logic of social inclusion: the state not only compensates people for insufficient income but also seeks to remove the barriers that prevent them from working, living independently, raising a child in a family, or remaining part of their community. This is the approach Ukraine must gradually adopt as part of its negotiations to join the European Union. This article explains what this means in practice, where Ukraine stands today, and what steps still need to be taken. The accession negotiations are divided into 33 thematic chapters. Social policy and employment fall under Chapter 19. In October 2026, the EU opened negotiations with Ukraine on this chapter and set out the conditions Ukraine must meet in this area . One of these conditions is that Ukraine must align its social protection and social inclusion system with EU rules and approaches and demonstrate that national and local authorities have the capacity to implement it in practice. This involves not only adopting legislation but also establishing mechanisms to implement it, including sufficient qualified personnel, capable institutions, and effective oversight. In its 2025 report , the European Commission assessed Ukraine as being at an early stage of preparation under Chapter 19. Among the specific tasks it identified were further reform of social benefits and the introduction of a new system for procuring social services. The assessment remained unchanged a year later: according to its 2026 report , Ukraine is still at an early stage of preparation, although the Commission notes some progress, particularly the adoption of the law on basic social assistance. At the same time, the Commission again identifies social benefits reform as a key priority. It considers the level of support insufficient, especially for people with disabilities and those in vulnerable situations. The EU’s negotiating position , adopted in October 2026 when negotiations on Chapter 19 were opened, sets out in detail the areas Ukraine should focus on in social protection and inclusion. There are five priorities: Strengthen the social protection system and access to it; Ensure children’s right to grow up in a family environment and develop services for children; Establish an accessible, high-quality long-term care system for everyone who needs it; Support people who care for family members; Continue the transition from institutional care to independent living in the community for people with disabilities. How do regional security conditions affect their capacity, and what do recent legislative changes mean for local development? Do municipalities have sufficient financial resources to perform their core functions? The September 2026 Municipal Review explores these and other questions. Key findings In September, some rules for strategic planning, local council operations, education funding and the preparation of public investment projects changed for local communities. Amendments to the State Regional Development Strategy provide for more differentiated support for municipalities, depending on whether they are classified as recovery territories, territories with special development conditions, growth poles or sustainable development territories. Parliament is considering draft laws to keep local councils operational under martial law and clarify the recall and replacement of councillors, reducing the risk of local government paralysis. Municipalities face higher education spending following the second stage of teacher pay increases and a change in the pay system away from the unified salary scale, new requirements for small schools, and the extension of free school meals to all pupils. Public investment increasingly requires projects to align with strategic priorities, meet climate and social criteria, be prepared for submission through DREAM, and comply with grant funding rules. These changes come amid a suspension of capital expenditure payments linked to a shortage of funds in the single treasury account. Local budgets’ own revenues again grew much faster than inflation, but payment restrictions mean that municipalities may not be able to use these resources when needed. General fund revenues excluding transfers rose by 25.6% year on year to UAH 44.7 billion, while inflation stood at 10%. Kyiv’s revenues increased 2.6-fold, reflecting a base effect: in September 2025, the city transferred UAH 8 billion to the state budget, which was a part of the corporate income tax paid to its budget by state-owned banks. Personal income tax remained the main revenue source, generating UAH 30.9 billion, up 20.1% from September 2025 as average wages increased. Revenues from land tax, the single tax and real estate tax increased too. Excise tax revenues were lower than a year earlier, despite growth over the first nine months. Transfers increased 3.6-fold, driven primarily by a 69.8% rise in the education subvention following two stages of teacher pay increases and the allocation of UAH 1.4 billion in additional grants to war-affected municipalities and regions. To maintain in-person education, or at least a hybrid format, educational institutions need additional funding for shelters. How has the government addressed these challenges? How much has education funding changed since the start of the full-scale invasion? Since 2022, Ukraine has received substantial international assistance, enabling it to finance civilian spending and some military expenditures. As Russia continues to devastate our economy, domestic revenues are declining, while the need for external support is growing. title: How Can We Help Local Communities Finance Reconstruction?
summary: Substantial domestic funds are available for borrowing by both the central government, through OVDPs, and local communities, through municipal bonds.
relevance_reason: Обсуждает возможность финансирования восстановления Украины через муниципальные облигации и ОВДП. Это конкретные финансовые инструменты и их потенциал.
full_text: Public finance October 29, 2026 How Can We Help Local Communities Finance Reconstruction? Illia Kyselov Public finance October 29, 2026 Facebook X Telegram 39 According to UN and World Bank estimates as of the end of 2025, rebuilding Ukraine will require at least $588 billion. Clearly, the state budget alone cannot cover such an amount. Meanwhile, Ukrainians currently hold approximately UAH 926 billion in cash outside the banking system and the equivalent of $117.6 billion in foreign currency cash. For comparison, individuals currently hold UAH 1.5 trillion in bank deposits and have invested UAH 159.3 billion in domestic government bonds (OVDPs). This suggests that substantial domestic funds are available for borrowing by both the central government, through OVDPs, and local communities, through municipal bonds. This financing instrument is widely used internationally but remains largely untapped in Ukraine. This article explores how local communities could make use of municipal bonds. How much do local communities borrow, and how? Ukrainian municipalities began issuing their own securities as early as the mid-1990s, but this financing instrument failed to gain widespread trust and, consequently, popularity. The unsuccessful experiences of Odesa and Kyiv likely undermined confidence in municipal bonds. In 1997, Odesa became the first city in Ukraine to issue bonds , raising UAH 60 million at an annual interest rate of 50%. In 1998, the newly elected mayor declared a default on those bonds, even though funds were available in the city’s accounts. The debt was not repaid until 2005. The problem, then, was more political than financial. No municipal bonds were issued after that until 2003. From that year onward, new bond issues required approval from the Ministry of Finance. In 2015, Kyiv suspended payments on Eurobonds issued in 2005 and 2011 worth more than $500 million and deferred payments on domestic bonds worth more than UAH 5 billion . This was due to the difficult situation in the country and the depreciation of the hryvnia (in 2014–2015, the exchange rate rose from approximately UAH 8 per dollar to more than UAH 30 per dollar). That same year, the government included Kyiv’s Eurobonds in a sovereign debt restructuring program carried out with IMF assistance: $550 million in Eurobonds were exchanged for government bonds , while the city was left with a debt of $175.5 million to the Ministry of Finance . The most comprehensive data on municipal bond issuance between 1995 and 2021 can be found in a U-LEAP report , which provides the basis for Table 1. According to these data, 19 cities issued bonds totaling UAH 16.9 billion during that period (in prices prevailing at the time, so the amount would be higher in today’s prices, though still relatively small: for comparison, local authorities borrowed nearly UAH 16 billion in just the first eight months of this year). title: Why Is It Harder for Internally Displaced People to Find a Job and How to Help Them?
summary: How can we help IDPs find employment and thus adapt faster to their new environment?
relevance_reason: Поднимает вопрос о трудностях трудоустройства внутренне перемещенных лиц в Украине и способах их решения. Это социальный и экономический аспект, связанный с последствиями конфликта.
full_text: Labor market October 22, 2026 Why Is It Harder for Internally Displaced People to Find a Job and How to Help Them? Karyna Skalova Mariia Holubieva Yehor Varlamov Labor market Photo: unsplash.com / Christin Hume October 22, 2026 Facebook X Telegram 54 Integration into the local labor market is one of the key components of successful adaptation for internally displaced persons (IDPs). However, IDPs cannot always quickly find jobs that match their experience and qualifications. How can we help IDPs find employment and thus adapt faster to their new environment? The full-scale war forced millions of Ukrainians to leave their homes. According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), a United Nations agency, the number of IDPs in Ukraine was estimated at 7.1 million in April 2022. Later, some of them returned home or moved abroad, and by June 2026, approximately 3.9 million IDPs were living in Ukraine, or roughly 13% of the population (according to the Institute for Demography, the population in Ukrainian government-controlled territory is estimated at approximately 29 million). Some 83% of IDPs have been displaced for more than a year, and 67% for more than two years. Some people were forced to flee their homes as early as 2014 or in subsequent years before the full-scale invasion. Internal displacement in Ukraine is therefore a long-term challenge. Therefore, a long-term solution is needed. The primary policy objective should be not merely to provide temporary housing and humanitarian assistance, but to integrate IDPs into their new communities, particularly through economic integration. This approach faces several challenges: regional differences in labor market structures, a shortage of affordable housing, and a lack of vacancies with flexible working hours. Differences in regional labor markets According to an IOM survey (June 2026), 72% of IDPs had moved outside their home oblast, while 27% had relocated within the same oblast. Meanwhile, 27% of IDPs had insufficient access to income-generating opportunities, and more than a third of displaced households reported having accepted lower-paying or lower-skilled jobs than those which they held before displacement. Earlier surveys show very similar results. In the May round of the IOM survey , with the same geographic distribution of displacement (72% having moved outside their home oblast and 27% within it), approximately 34% of IDPs reported a lack of income-generating opportunities, while the share of those who had been forced to accept lower-paying jobs was 28%. Displacement patterns were similar in January , when 71% had moved to other oblasts and 28% had remained within their home oblast. At that time, 32% of IDPs reported difficulties finding employment, while 30% had been forced to take lower-skilled or lower-paying jobs. The announcement signalled the apparent end of a six-week government counteroffensive to reclaim the coast near the mouth of the Red Sea, seized by the Houthis in September in a lightning advance that squeezed oil exports. Sunday's announcement of a government retreat raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden, and underscores the predicament faced by Saudi Arabia in trying to stop the Houthis' drone and missile attacks on the kingdom. The government forces have been based in Aden on the southern coast since 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa. Houthi gains in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping in recent months have strengthened the position of Iran in the wider Middle East conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February. "The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate," the main military force fighting for Yemen's government in the south of the country said in a statement. "This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats." There was no immediate response from the Houthis, or from Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government's main international ally. HOUTHI GAINS Yemen's decade-long civil war, which had been dormant since 2022, abruptly reignited this summer as a spillover from the Iran conflict. The Houthis made rapid gains to capture the coast along the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that controls access to it, while besieging government forces in Taiz, the country's third-biggest city, in mountains above the approach to Aden. A Saudi-backed government offensive last month rapidly retook key positions around the strait, notably Dhubab, but failed to drive the Houthis entirely away from the area or to retake the city of al-Mocha further up the coast. The Houthis have responded by intensifying drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, grounding flights with strikes on its main airports as well as setting global energy markets on edge by targeting energy facilities. They also made significant advances in the highland areas north of Aden, cutting off Taiz in early October and putting increased pressure on the disparate coalition of forces fighting for the internationally recognised government.
